questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [senior] repair, then constrain: moving data rules into the database on a live table (opusorganize, apprenticeship/curriculum/07). Scenario: a multi-tenant task tracker had a SEV-2 in which a user from another organisation was set as a task's assignee, because the assignee column has a plain single-column foreign key to users. The fix review asks for three rules in the database itself: an assignee must be a member of the task's own organisation; every task must have an organisation (about 2% of the 6.8M Task rows have none, left over from an old import); and task numbers must be unique per organisation (about 1,100 duplicate pairs exist from an old race). The table takes about 900 writes/s at peak, the business tolerates about 500 ms of blocked writes, deploys are rolling with old machines serving after the release-phase migration, and the previous release must stay a safe rollback target. Write your plan before you look: how you find and repair the existing violations, the constraint each rule becomes, the order and form in which each one is added, what old binaries can still write in the meantime, and what the API returns once the database refuses a write. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] Starts by measuring the damage with queries rather than with DDL: tasks whose assignee is not a member of the task's organisation, tasks with no organisation, and duplicate numbers per organisation. What each repair means is a product decision (unassign and notify, derive the organisation from the project, renumber the later duplicate), and it is settled before any constraint ships.

[w3] The membership rule becomes a compound foreign key: the task's (assignee, organisation) pair must reference the membership table's (user, organisation) pair, which first needs a unique key on that pair to point at. The database then refuses a stranger as assignee even when a script or a new code path skips the service's check.

[w3] Each foreign key or check goes on in two steps: added NOT VALID, which checks every new write from that moment but skips the rows already there, then validated in a later step that scans the table without blocking writes. Added this way (PostgreSQL ALTER TABLE semantics), the constraint stops new violations at once while the old rows are repaired behind it. Under the default MATCH SIMPLE a row whose organisation is null is not checked at all, and the organisation backfill is itself an UPDATE the new key checks, so the order is: repair those rows' foreign assignees, backfill the organisation, then VALIDATE.

[w3] NOT NULL arrives last and indirectly: backfill the missing organisations, add a CHECK that the column is not null as NOT VALID, validate it, and only then set the column NOT NULL, which (from PostgreSQL 12) can rely on the validated check instead of scanning 6.8M rows under a lock that blocks reads and writes.
keyPoints.quote: `NOT NULL` on a big table needs a default or a validated `CHECK` first.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Uniqueness comes after the duplicates are gone: build the unique index on (organisation, number) without blocking writes, then attach it as the constraint. If a duplicate slips in during the build, the build fails and leaves an invalid index that still costs every write until it is dropped, so the plan checks for one and retries.

[w2] Old binaries keep serving after the migration runs, so each enforcement step ships only once no running machine and no rollback target can still produce the violation it forbids: the code that always sets the organisation, and that checks the assignee, goes out one full release before the rule it relies on.

[w2] The incident's relation is rarely the only one: every other reference to a user on a tenant table (reporter, watcher, owner) gets the same compound form, and a schema lint flags any relation on a tenant table that does not include the organisation column.
[w1] The proof is a regression test that goes around the repository: a raw SQL insert of a cross-organisation assignee must be rejected by the database, not merely by the service.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — the constraint release goes out like this: the compound foreign key is added fully validated inside the release-phase migration while about 3,800 cross-organisation assignees are still in the table; the duplicate-number cleanup ran on Friday and the unique index build started on Monday; the NOT NULL is a plain SET NOT NULL in the same migration; old machines keep creating tasks through a path that leaves the organisation empty for twenty minutes; and the API now answers 409 when someone picks an assignee from another organisation. What breaks, who notices first, and what in your plan prevents it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] On dirty data the validated add cannot succeed: after its write-blocking scan it meets the first of the 3,800 bad rows and the release-phase migration fails, which aborts the whole deploy. The release that was meant to ship the writer fix and the repair ships nothing, and new cross-organisation assignments keep landing meanwhile; adding the key NOT VALID in that release would have stopped them at once.

[w3] Between Friday and Monday the race that produced the duplicates kept running, so the index build fails on a fresh duplicate and leaves an invalid index behind. Close the race at its source first (number allocation done atomically by the database, not read-then-write in the service), then clean up, then build, close together in time; a failed online build is dropped before the retry (PostgreSQL CREATE INDEX semantics).

[w3] A plain SET NOT NULL scans all 6.8M rows under the strongest lock, so every read and write on the table waits for the whole scan, far past the 500 ms budget; and if any null is left (an old machine inserted one after the backfill), the statement fails only after that long scan.

[w2] Once the column is required, the old create path fails with 500s for as long as old machines serve, and a column default cannot derive the right organisation. Ship the writer first and wait a release, or fill the column from the project with a trigger during the window; the enforcement waits for both the running version and the rollback target.
keyPoints.quote: the one you might roll back to

keyPoints.text: [w2] 409 is the wrong answer for a foreign assignee: it tells the client to refresh and retry, while the request itself is invalid. Map the foreign-key refusal to a 400 or 422 that names the field, and word it so the response does not reveal whether that user exists in another organisation.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your plan against the alternatives: repairing all the data before adding any constraint versus adding the constraint NOT VALID first and repairing behind it; a compound foreign key versus an application-level membership check versus row-level security; unassigning foreign assignees versus adding those users to the task's organisation; and enforcing required fields in the database versus only in the request schema. Also say what the fix changes for API clients. For each, say what you bought, what it cost, and which requirement put you on that side.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Repairing first puts the constraint on clean data in one step, but new violations keep arriving while the repair runs; NOT VALID first stops them immediately, at the cost of refusing writes from any code path that still produces them, which is why it waits until those paths are gone.

[w3] A compound foreign key holds for every writer, raw SQL and scripts included, and costs an extra unique key on the parent plus a composite relation the ORM has to model; an application check is flexible and easy to bypass; row-level security also covers reads, which foreign keys never do, at the price of a non-superuser runtime role and per-transaction tenant plumbing.

[w2] Unassigning a foreign assignee is safe and reversible (keep the old value in the repair log) but leaves the task without an owner; making the stranger a member of the organisation would fix the integrity error by granting access that nobody approved, so integrity repairs never widen access.

[w2] The request schema rejects bad input early with useful messages, but only on the API path; the database constraint also covers imports, scripts and old binaries. Keep both, with the database as the backstop and the schema for the error message.

[w1] Moving a rule into the database changes the API contract: requests that used to succeed now fail with a new status and body, which in the lab broke the change's own test (a 404 became a 400 and the assignee field became nested), so the change is announced and the clients' tests are updated with it.
